description:
Me presento

¡Hola! Soy Denzel, estudiante de Ingeniería en Sistemas Computacionales en el Instituto Tecnológico de Zacatepec, y me encantaría que formaras parte de mi equipo, In Sync. Me interesan los datos geoespaciales y el desarrollo web. Para el reto de armonización de MODIS y VIIRS ya investigué los datos que se encuentran disponibles de NASA FIRMS y tengo una idea clara para el proyecto y como podemos ejecutarla con exito.
summary: Satellites have tracked fire hotspots for over two decades, but the record has been split between MODIS (2000–present) and VIIRS (2012–present), whose counts cannot be compared directly since VIIRS detects about 3.7x more hotspots. Heat Atlas harmonizes both records into one consistent time series across the Americas (80 million detections) and transforms it into an interactive burning activity calendar. Users can select any region, analyze monthly historical trends since 2002, compare anomalies against historical medians, and download the raw data. Updated daily via NASA FIRMS, this tool bridges the gap for regional fire management.
details:
Heat Atlas is a web application that harmonizes over two decades of active fire records across the 35 countries of the Americas—totaling 80 million detections—into one continuous and reliable time series. Using NASA FIRMS active fire data, we compare MODIS Aqua (2000–present) and VIIRS Suomi-NPP (2012–present), which pass over at the same local time (~13:30). To ensure both sensors measure the exact same phenomenon, our pipeline removes persistent industrial heat sources (such as refineries and gas flares) along with low-confidence detections, counting "fire cell-days" on a standardized 1 km grid. A monthly calibration factor per country, computed over the 2012–2025 overlap period, converts historical MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent units. This factor is lowest during each region's peak fire season and highest during the rainy season, when smaller fires dominate. In leave-one-year-out cross-validation, this monthly calibration reduces mean error from 15.6% to 11.3% in Mexico (r = 0.988) and to 10.1% in Brazil (r = 0.992).

A consistent fire history from 2002 to today reveals real seasonal patterns and ecological anomalies instead of artificial sensor jumps. Civil protection agencies, forestry institutions like CONAFOR, fire brigades, and researchers can pinpoint when their local fire season starts and peaks, compare any current month against a normal year, and spot unusual wildfire activity early for any custom area they select.

Under the hood, a Python data pipeline combined with a FastAPI and DuckDB backend serves the harmonized dataset and refreshes recent hotspots daily, filling S-NPP gaps with NOAA-20 data clearly flagged as preliminary. This powers a lightweight web interface deployed on Vercel, built with MapLibre GL for the interactive 3D globe, H3 spatial hexagons, and D3.js charts, alongside open geographic layers from Natural Earth and OpenStreetMap (via OpenFreeMap). What makes Heat Atlas especially creative is how it turns complex multi-sensor remote-sensing calibration into an intuitive visual experience, pairing a 3D globe with a granular "burn calendar" heatmap and direct CSV exports. Throughout development, our team carefully accounted for orbital overpass alignment, spatial resolution bias (1 km vs. 375 m), industrial false positives, UTC time standardization, preliminary data transparency, and the open disclosure of AI-assisted coding.
dataRefs: MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m (S-NPP, NOAA20)
